items.title: Nothing offers a full look at its AI earbuds and charging case
items.summary: Nothing is showing off a much more detailed look at its upcoming AI earbuds ahead of their December 8th release. The Ear Note buds can record your calls, while their charging case can record, transcribe, and summarize your conversations. Like the Ear 3, the Ear Note's microphone-
items.content:
The Ear Note buds look similar to Nothing’s previous earbuds, but now their case doubles as an AI-connected note taker for conversations.

Nothing is showing off a much more detailed look at its upcoming AI earbuds ahead of their December 8th release. The Ear Note buds can record your calls, while their charging case can record, transcribe, and summarize your conversations.

Like the Ear 3 , the Ear Note’s microphone-equipped case comes with a “Talk” button that you can use to record your own voice. There’s also a new “Record” button that can record and transcribe your conversations. In a post on X , Nothing CEO Carl Pei says the button will allow you to record calls through the earbuds, and meetings through the case as a “first step toward a hardware context layer for AI.”

As previously reported by Bloomberg , the buds will connect to an app where you can manage recordings, transcriptions, and AI summaries. They’ll also “support interactions with various AI agents, including a more basic voice-control system developed by Nothing, letting users engage in back-and-forth conversations,” according to Bloomberg .

The Ear Note buds themselves look similar to the Ear 3 and Ear 3A, but come with Nothing’s “best in-ear audio to date.” The new device, which Nothing teased earlier this month , will join some of the other AI-powered note-taking devices we’ve seen emerge recently, such as the Amazon Bee and the Plaud Note Pro . Apple also brought AI capabilities to its Watch Series 12, allowing Siri to listen to your conversations and generate recaps.

items.title: Art of play in the age of AI
items.summary: Now that code ships faster than ever, you have more time to spend on projects just for the fun of it. Here's what we can learn through that process as developers. The post Art of play in the age of AI appeared first on The GitHub Blog .
items.content:
As kids, we spent hours tinkering and building and just messing with things. As an adult, I could watch my own young kiddos figure out how certain shapes and movement work all day. Through that play, we improved our problem-solving and language skills, and it’s probably not a stretch to say it was good for our early engineering skills.

In this era of development now, we’re starting to get a taste of that again. We’re experimenting more, and taking in more changes, because it’s all new!

For the last four years at GitHub Universe, we’ve had hackable conference badges. What started as a simple e-ink display for your name and job title morphed into a labor of love for Martin Woodward , VP of Developer Relations. This year, the badge evolved into a device with a color screen, rechargeable battery, accelerometer sensors, and touch-sensitive gaming controls.

The tinkering we’ve seen with the badges has been amazing.

Hacking the GitHub Universe Badge with these 3 apps that I made!! #GitHubUniverse https://t.co/Qy5wYPqXf5

you can play octo drive on your @github universe badge! repo - https://t.co/DrYkhjvMVt https://t.co/S6jVwxPdEY

According to the Octoverse report, 40% of pull requests were started by agents by September. That’s a big jump from the 17% we saw in March, which was already a pretty high number.

With that kind of pace of change, it’s easy to feel unsteady thinking about our coding skills that we’ve been honing as an industry for decades. At the same time, one might argue that the tools and changes in front of us offer more room for experimentation and creativity!

AI can turn our ideas into working code faster than ever before. We can build things just because we’re curious to see if it’ll work, without the burden of figuring out every single step before getting started. The learning is moving to different parts of the building timeline.

As Martin said in our GitHub Podcast episode, “Give yourself permission to play, call it learning,” but with the caveat that you should time-box it so that you don’t spend too much time perfecting it. Know when to stop, ship, and share.

What’s really exciting is how the scope of projects have changed. With AI tooling, we don’t have to build with everyone in mind every time (not that we necessarily did before, but it was definitely a default mindset for the industry). We can build things way more often for our exact use cases. It could “just work on my machine” and be feature-complete!

At the GitHub Universe closing keynote, Martin wanted to teach himself machine learning, so he built himself a pedometer onto his conference badge. He used Copilot to collect movement data from the badge’s accelerometer, trained a simple machine-learning model in his browser, and deployed it to the badge. Then he walked around to test whether it could tell the difference between walking, standing still, and fidgeting.

Imagine just a year or two ago wanting to dabble with machine learning. You totally could have! But for the average developer, that’s a daunting task. The barrier to entry for so many tougher concepts has gotten lower, and that means more people can experiment and have fun with any device they can think of, from a conference badge to a smart picture frame to a home TV.

AI is top of mind all the time right now, but you are a part of the story, too.

In order to scale with AI, we need human judgement. We can see the AI tells in writing (“that’s the real unlock!”), in imagery (the fonts, man), or in code (commenting code blocks that have never been commented before). We need to keep the feedback loop, to be able to inspect, debug, and test what the agent produced, and to make whatever we’re building our own.

It’s really fun to share your experiments with the world, but contributing to existing open source projects take a bit more consideration than that. Both our podcast episode and the keynote addressed this. We’re seeing maintainers get absolutely hammered with AI-powered contributions to their repositories, which adds a lot to the maintenance burden.

Efforts need to be made by all of us, like the one shared here , to help ease burdens for maintainers.

As Martin explained in the keynote, “Open source is the freedom to inspect, to remix, and to share without asking for permission. But it’s not the freedom to impose your will on others.”

Forking a repository gives you room to explore your own ideas, and there’s a really fun, exciting power in that. But before you impose those ideas on others and send them to the main repository, make sure you:

Respecting that work helps keep open source manageable (and even enjoyable) for the people looking after it.

We answered the perennial question on our badge, “But can it run Doom?” Why yes, yes it does. Give it a go on our virtual badge , and try tinkering on it yourself.

Then get your hands on your own badge . We made some extra badges just for you. Order yours today, then tell us what you’ll be building. Plus, use code FREESHIPBLOG26 for free standard shipping through December 1, 2026.

items.title: Lead azide detonation sends clouds over Iowa as questions of health risks swirl
items.summary: Prior modeling estimated the plume would cover hundreds of square miles.
items.content:
In a powerful explosion that launched gray-white clouds over southeastern Iowa, the Army detonated 68 barrels containing 9,700 pounds (4.4 tons) of degraded lead azide on Wednesday at about 9 am CT, preventing a spontaneous unmitigated explosion of the crystallized, highly unstable compound.

The detonation occurred at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant (IAAAP) in Middletown, Iowa, a town of less than 400 people. Residents within a 5-mile area of the facility were advised to evacuate, while people farther out were told to shelter in place, close windows and doors tightly, turn off fans, and set indoor air systems to recirculate.

Local Iowa outlet KWQC caught the plume from the two earth-covered containers, which were detonated simultaneously. A KWQZ journalist, at a reportedly safe distance from the blast, said on the live broadcast that he could see and then feel the shockwave roll through the crop field in which he was standing. He put a mask on for the rest of the broadcast.

Lead is a neurotoxin that does not break down in the environment and poses significant health risks, particularly to young children and pregnant people.

In the hours leading to the detonation, the Army released maps showing modeled drift and distribution of the plume. They indicated that airborne lead would travel around 100 miles to the southwest of the facility, while dust deposition would cover around 200 square miles in that direction. Researchers and government workers have already collected air and soil samples from the area, which will act as baseline readings for lead levels in the aftermath and fallout of the detonation.

In preparation for the blast, the Army surrounded the earth-covered containers with sand-and lime fill. They set up water cannons and misters intended to keep dust down. They also covered the top of the container with fire-suppressant foam. The Army documented the efforts with a video posted to social media Wednesday morning .

The explosion follows days of confusion, outrage, questions, and delays. Although the Army said that it has known about the hazardous state of the lead azide since March, Iowans were largely unaware of the situation and the planned detonation until last week. At that time, the Army had planned to detonate the barrels on Friday, November 20. But public alarm and an emergency court filing from environmental groups led to a delay, which was initially scheduled for Monday, then Tuesday, and finally to today.

A federal appeals court initially issued a stay on the Army’s permit to conduct the detonation, and, on Monday, Trump said he ordered the military to halt the operation until the court lifted the stay and Governor-elect Rob Sand, a Democrat, signed off. Ultimately, the court ruled this week that the Army could move ahead with plans, given no better option.

But questions continue to swirl about how the lead azide got to such a “catastrophically hazardous condition.” On Tuesday, The Washington Post reported that it had viewed emails that suggest the Army knew since at least September 2025, not this past March.

items.title: The Verge’s guide to affordable holiday gifts under $25
items.summary: Gift-giving on a tight budget is tough, but constraints can also encourage some creative thinking. We thought for a long while (and asked other Verge staffers) about the best items out there, and we're pretty happy with what we came up with. For this list, we've rounded up a barr
items.content:
Whether it’s stocking stuffers or a little treat for yourself, these are some of our favorite gifts under $25.

If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

Gift-giving on a tight budget is tough, but constraints can also encourage some creative thinking. We thought for a long while (and asked other Verge staffers) about the best items out there, and we’re pretty happy with what we came up with.

For this list, we’ve rounded up a barrage of fun gadgets and stocking-stuffer specials. You’ll find nostalgic ways to spruce up a room like Play-Doh’s Blooms , fancy ways to jot down notes like the Pilot Kakuno fountain pen , and plenty of tech-forward extras like the Time Timer Mod . It’s time to get creative with your budget buys, and this list can get you there.

Lamicall’s magnetic cord organizers are simple yet effective tools. They hold the ends of your most frequently used cables so they don’t fall to the floor when you unplug them, and the low-cost accessories can be stuck to the side of your desk or kitchen counter. They also work great behind your entertainment center or wherever else is convenient.

There’s regular Play-Doh for kids, but did you know that Play-Doh makes kits for adults, too? We’re not scoffing. The new Blooms sets take on Lego’s floral bouquets with more realistic-looking flower arrangements, and they include a vase. They’re equal parts nostalgic kitsch and stylish decor.

For visual learners, a visible timeline can help keep the pace moving. The Time Timer Mod provides an aesthetically pleasing 60-minute countdown to help your favorite procrastinator stay on task and maximize efficiency, no matter what they’re working on.

Smart plugs are the easiest way to bring older electronics into the 21st century. For the smart home fan in your life, TP-Link’s Kasa plugs are a brilliant budget-friendly buy, adding Google or Amazon Alexa voice assistance to everyday items, not to mention power schedules and remote control. Note: They support 2.4GHz Wi-Fi connectivity only.

For the giftee who likes to keep things on the level (literally), this striking 12-inch leveling tool offers the traditional bubble measure alongside LED lights that turn from red when the level needs adjusting to green when it locks in. It’s just a slightly more satisfying way to ensure you’re level before drilling or hammering.

Sometimes a little change can make a big difference. Aothia’s desk mats bring aesthetic and functional improvements in an array of stylish color options, with a smooth faux leather surface that protects your desktop and can bring some much-needed order to your desk layout.

These magnetic word tiles are a classic for a reason. Sure, silly phrases or profound thoughts on a fridge door won’t change the world, but they could brighten a housemate’s day. If anything, slowing down a few times a day to read these fun messages as you open the fridge is a welcome break that we all could use.

If you’ve got a scribe on your list who prefers the feel of paper instead of digital screens, give their pencils or fountain pens something to dig into with the Midori MD Note pad. Cream-colored paper, wide lines, and 185-degree binding combine for a great way to jot down anything that comes to mind.

These dimmable, color-changing bulbs offer Wi-Fi connection, simple setup, and Matter compatibility so they can seamlessly fit into Google Home, Amazon Alexa, Samsung SmartThings, and Apple Home smart home systems. Best of all, these smart features come at a price that makes buying multipacks more affordable than other brands.

These Ikea pegboards are a great gift for anyone looking to organize a bedroom, office, or dorm room. They’re available in multiple sizes and colors, and they can be presented in your space in multiple ways, be it mounted on the wall or stood on a desk. Extra accessories make it even easier to organize doodads.

The comedy streaming service created by CollegeHumor alumni offers endless, ad-free entertainment for the improv lover in your life. With multiple shows from some of the top names in comedy, and a business model that encourages profit sharing for creators, it’s a feel-good way to bring more laughter to someone’s life.

Everyone needs a good flashlight, and perhaps your recipient’s next one should ditch the replaceable batteries. Wuben’s rechargeable G5 has a pocketable, spy-tech-inspired design, USB-C charging, and adjustable brightness. More importantly, the 400-lumen light is super compact, making it easy to stow or clip onto your bag.

Not all reusable water bottles are created equal. Give the gift of a narrow-mouthed bottle, like this 16-ounce Nalgene pick, which makes it easy to take measured sips on the go. Take this advice from someone (me) who bought the wide-mouthed version and regularly spills water all over themself.

This moldable material is more than just glue. It’s useful for practical tasks, like fixing drywall, crafting your own cable management system, or just to build for fun. Sugru glue comes in multiple colors and serves as a smart solution to any number of household problems, especially for people who don’t have access to a 3D printer.

This once-futuristic automatic soap dispenser has become affordable enough for anyone to own. This particular model is one that a Verge staffer owns and likes, thanks to its customizable portions for the perfect hands-free wash. It’s especially great if you cook a lot and don’t want to touch your soap dispenser.

For the chef on your list, these convenient garlic peelers make it easy to strip off the skin without crushing the cloves. In other words, it does the most annoying part of dealing with garlic on your behalf. If only it were this easy to tell them they need to take the garlic down a notch in their red sauce.
